physical_harm: several injuries and asphyxia due to throttling
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the chain of circumstantial evidence, including the inquest report, post-mortem findings, and the appellant's failure to explain the injuries and circumstances surrounding the death of his wife.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as unreliable, noting their fabricated accounts about the victim's illness and hospitalization, which were found to be false and inconsistent with the physical evidence.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant absconded after the incident and was arrested two days later at a distant place, which the court considered as part of the circumstantial evidence pointing to his guilt.
investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed against the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 302 IPC

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted the appellant of the offence under Section 302 IPC
appeal_history.high_court: Dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the victim, the appellant's wife, died due to asphyxia caused by throttling, and the appellant failed to explain the injuries sustained by the deceased while living with him. The prosecution discharged its burden by establishing a chain of circumstances pointing to the appellant's guilt.
defence_argument: The defence contended that the witnesses PW-1 to PW-6 claimed the victim died in the hospital due to illness, and the prosecution failed to prove motive. They also questioned the reliability of the inquest report and the place of the incident.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principle under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, which holds that if the accused fails to explain incriminating circumstances or provides false explanations, such omissions and falsehoods become additional links in the chain of circumstances.
precedent_relied_upon: Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra (2006) 10 SCC 681; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Balaji Gunthu Dhule v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 11 SCC 685; Nagendra Sah v. State of Bihar (2021) 10 SCC 725; Gargi v. State of Haryana (2019) 9 SCC 738; Shivaji Chintappa Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021) 3 SCALE 384; Anwar Ali and Anr. v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020) 10 SCC 166; Jose Alias Pappachan v. Sub-Inspector of Police, Koyilandy and Anr. (2016) 10 SCC 519; Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1957 SC 637; Alber Oraon v. State of Jharkhand (2014) 12 SCC 306; Sudru v. State of Chhattisgarh (2019) 8 SCC 333; Ujjagar Singh v. State of Punjab (2007) 13 SCC 90; Vivek Kalra v. State of Rajasthan (2014) 12 SCC 439; Pappu v. The State of Uttar Pradesh (2022) SCC OnLine SC 176; Hanumant v. State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1952 SC 343; Sabitri Samantaray v. State of Odisha (2022) SCC OnLine SC 673
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence of life imprisonment was imposed because the prosecution established a complete chain of circumstances proving the appellant's guilt beyond any doubt, and the appellant failed to provide credible explanations for the circumstances surrounding the victim's death.
